stimulus.text: Two engravings from Theodor de Bry's America series (1591), after drawings by Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues. The first shows Florida Indians planting seeds of beans and maize in cleared fields. The second shows the same people hunting deer disguised under deerskins. De Bry never visited North America; he engraved the scenes in Europe from watercolors painted by Jacques Le Moyne, a French artist with the Laudonnière expedition.

stem: The engravings were made by Theodor de Bry, a European artist who never visited North America, working from watercolors painted by Jacques Le Moyne, a French artist with the Laudonnière expedition. What is the most important limitation of these engravings as historical evidence?

options.text: They prove that every Native society farmed in exactly the same way.
options.misconception: Treats two engravings of one region as proof about a whole continent.

options.text: They were made long after all Native societies in the region had disappeared.
options.misconception: Puts the 1591 engravings after societies that were still alive then.

options.text: They show Native life through European eyes and may carry European assumptions.
They hold no information that historians can reliably use at all.
options.misconception: Throws out a source for being mediated instead of reading it with care.

rationales.A: Two engravings of one region cannot prove uniformity across a continent, whatever they show.
rationales.B: The engravings date to 1591, when these societies were very much alive, so disappearance cannot be the limitation.
rationales.C: De Bry never saw the people he engraved, so his scenes filter Native life through European eyes and may reflect European assumptions.
rationales.D: A mediated source still holds usable evidence when read with care, so it is wrong to discard the engravings entirely.
rationales.general:
1. Name the maker. Theodor de Bry engraved the scenes, and he never visited North America.
2. Trace the chain. He worked from watercolors by Jacques Le Moyne, a French artist with the Laudonnière expedition, for readers in Europe.
3. See the chain as a game of telephone across an ocean. Each hand in the chain can bend a pose, a dress, or a setting toward what Europeans expected to see.
4. Ask what still stands. Used with care, the images still show real practices like planting and hunting.
Remember: always ask who made a source and who it was made for before you trust its details.
